title: A First Information Report (FIR) under Section 173 BNSS (formerly Section 154 CrPC) is the earliest information recorded by the police regarding a cognizable offence

content.overview: An FIR is the information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence recorded by the officer in charge of a police station under section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, formerly section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The informant gives the information; the police record it, read it over, and take a signature. Section 173 also provides for information given by electronic communication, and for a preliminary enquiry in a limited class of offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven years, with prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, to be completed within fourteen days. Zero FIR is the practice, now reflected in the section 173 framework, of registering information even if the offence was committed outside the territorial limits of that station. This topic is the informant's format, not the later charge sheet.
content.short: A First Information Report (FIR) under Section 173 BNSS (formerly Section 154 CrPC) is the earliest information recorded by the police regarding a cognizable offence. It sets the criminal investigation mechanism in motion and incorporates new statutory mandates on e-FIR, Zero FIR, and 14-day preliminary enquiry.
content.detailed:
Core Drafting Skeleton & Statutory Rules for FIR under Section 173 BNSS

1. Addressee & Station Details
   • To: The Officer-in-Charge / Station House Officer (SHO)
   • Police Station: [Name of Police Station, District, State]

2. Informant / Complainant Details
   • Full name, father's/spouse's name, age, permanent & current address, contact number, and email.
   • If informant is an eye-witness, victim, or public officer.

3. Details of Occurrence & Locus
   • Date and precise time of the offence.
   • Place of occurrence (exact landmark, physical distance and direction from the Police Station).
   • Any delay in reporting explained upfront (to negate allegations of concoction or afterthought: Lalita Kumari).

4. Accused Identity & Roles
   • Names, parentage, addresses, and physical descriptions of accused persons.
   • If unknown: physical features, estimated age, attire, dialect, and identifiable marks.
   • Distinct overt acts performed by each accused (who assaulted, who brandished weapons, who threatened, who facilitated escape).

5. Narrative of the Offence (Chronological Statement)
   • Pre-incident circumstances, initial verbal altercation, or pre-existing enmity.
   • Weapon details (lathi, iron rod, firearm, knife).
   • Nature of injuries sustained and names of hospital / attending doctor / MLC numbers.
   • List of stolen/damaged property with estimated values.

6. Independent Witnesses
   • Names, addresses, and contact numbers of bystander witnesses who witnessed the crime.

7. Prayer / Demand for Investigation
   • Registration of regular FIR under relevant sections of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (e.g., BNS ss. 115, 118, 303, 351).
   • Apprehension of accused, recovery of weapons/articles, and medical examination of victim.

8. Signature / Left Thumb Impression (LTI) & Date

Key Statutory Changes under BNSS, 2023:
• e-FIR & Electronic Transmission (Section 173(1)): Information may be sent electronically; it must be signed within three days by the informant before being taken on formal record.
• Zero FIR: Police station must record information of any cognizable offence irrespective of territorial jurisdiction, take preventive steps, and transfer it to the jurisdictional station.
• Preliminary Enquiry (Section 173(3)): For offences punishable between 3 and 7 years, an enquiry may be conducted within 14 days with prior permission of an officer not below DSP rank to check prima facie substance.
• Remediating Police Refusal:
  - Section 173(4) BNSS (formerly 154(3) CrPC): Forward complaint to Superintendent of Police (SP).
  - Section 175(3) & 175(4) BNSS (formerly 156(3) CrPC): Application to Magistrate with mandatory supporting affidavit of compliance with SP representation.

cases.name: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
cases.holding: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC (now s. 173 BNSS) if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence; no preliminary enquiry is permissible in such cases except in 5 defined classes.
cases.relevance: Rule of mandatory FIR registration and strict guidelines on preliminary enquiry.

cases.name: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
cases.holding: Established seven famous illustrative categories where an FIR and criminal proceedings can be quashed by the High Court under inherent powers to prevent abuse of process.
cases.relevance: Grounds for quashing FIR under Section 528 BNSS (s. 482 CrPC).

cases.name: Youth Bar Association of India v. Union of India
cases.holding: Directed that copies of FIRs must be uploaded on police/state government websites within 24 to 48 hours of registration, except in sensitive matters such as sexual offences or terrorism.
cases.relevance: Transparency and prompt access to FIRs for bail and defense preparation.

examTips: Section 173(1) BNSS e-FIR requirement: Must be signed by the informant within three days.
Section 173(3) BNSS allows preliminary enquiry only for offences carrying 3 to 7 years imprisonment, capped at 14 days.
Under Section 175(4) BNSS, a Magistrate application under 175(3) must be accompanied by an affidavit of compliance with s. 173(4) (codifying Priyanka Srivastava).
FIR is not substantive evidence; it can only be used under BSA Sections 148 & 157 (ss. 145 & 155 IEA) for contradiction and corroboration of the informant.

enhancement.definition: An FIR format is the informant's account of a cognizable offence, given so the officer in charge can record it under section 173 BNSS.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The FIR sets investigation in motion. It is not evidence of guilt by itself, and it is not the final report. The section applies to cognizable offences.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: BNSS section 173, corresponding to CrPC section 154. Preliminary enquiry and electronic information are parts of section 173 and should be checked against the official text before a subsection is cited in court.
essentialIngredients: Signature after it is read over
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The format opens with the police station or the electronic mode, the informant's identity, and a statement that the information concerns a cognizable offence. The narrative is factual: what happened, when, where, who was present, and what was lost or injured. Argument and witness opinion do not belong in the first information. Section 173 requires the information to be reduced to writing and signed after it is read over. Electronic communication is signed or confirmed in the manner the section provides. If the offence is in the three-to-seven-year band, the statute allows a preliminary enquiry only with the prior permission of a Deputy Superintendent of Police or above and within fourteen days; that enquiry is not a refusal to record a cognizable case outside that band. Zero FIR means the station records the information even if the crime is outside its limits and then transfers it. A non-cognizable report is a different entry.
examples: Theft at a railway station is recorded at the station where the informant arrives, even if the theft was in another district, and is then transferred.
An email alleges a cognizable cheating offence. It is brought on the section 173 record rather than left in an inbox.
A neighbour disputes a boundary wall with no cognizable offence. An FIR format is the wrong instrument.
enhancement.problemApplication: Ask whether the facts disclose a cognizable offence. If yes, draft facts, place and time, and the section 173 recording steps. If the only issue is a civil debt, do not use this format.

keyTakeaways: Section 173 BNSS is the FIR provision, formerly section 154 CrPC.
It is for a cognizable offence.
The informant signs after the record is read over.
Electronic information and out-of-jurisdiction recording are section 173 issues.
An FIR is not a charge sheet.
authoritativeSources: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, section 154, as the former corresponding provision

verification.note: Section 173 correspondence and the fourteen-day preliminary-enquiry band are stated from the BNSS framework and flagged for subsection verification. No case citation added.

content.study: Use section 173 only for a cognizable offence. State facts, place, time and accused if known. Do not argue guilt. Electronic information still has to be taken on record as the section requires. A non-cognizable allegation is not forced into an FIR format.
